title: First Aid & Emergency Care
description: A practical course in helping someone during the first minutes of a medical emergency, before professional responders arrive. You will learn to assess a scene, perform hands-only CPR, control bleeding, and recognize conditions like stroke, anaphylaxis, and heat stroke. This course teaches first-responder basics only; it does not replace certified CPR/first aid training or professional medical care.
outcomes: You can check scene safety and a person's responsiveness and breathing before acting, and call 911 with the right information.
You can perform hands-only CPR and use an AED on an adult in cardiac arrest.
You can control severe bleeding with direct pressure, wound packing, and a tourniquet when needed.
You can recognize and respond to choking, anaphylaxis, seizures, and stroke using the FAST test.
You can treat burns, sprains, and fractures, and recognize heat and cold emergencies.
You can recognize opioid overdose and poisoning emergencies and assemble a usable first aid kit.

units.title: The First Aid Foundation
units.summary: Before you can help anyone, you need a framework: keep yourself safe, know what to check, and know how to get real help moving. This unit builds that foundation.

lessons.title: Check, Call, Care: Scene Safety First
lessons.intro: Every first aid emergency starts the same way, whether it is a skinned knee or a cardiac arrest: you look before you touch. The Check-Call-Care framework used by the American Red Cross keeps you from becoming a second victim and makes sure real help is already on the way while you act.

sections.heading: Check the Scene Before You Check the Person
body: Before you approach anyone, scan for danger: traffic, fire, downed power lines, gas smells, unstable structures, or an aggressive bystander. If the scene is not safe, you do not enter it. A first responder who becomes a second casualty helps no one, and now two people need rescue instead of one.

Once the scene looks safe, check the person for consciousness. Tap their shoulder firmly and ask loudly, "Are you okay?" If there is no response, treat this as a medical emergency and move to the Call step immediately. If they respond, ask what happened and whether they want help; a conscious adult can refuse care.

sections.heading: Protecting Yourself: Universal Precautions
body: Blood and body fluids can carry infection, so whenever possible put on disposable gloves before touching a wound, and use a CPR face shield or mask before giving rescue breaths. If you have no gloves, use a clean cloth, plastic bag, or the injured person's own hand to add a barrier.

Wash your hands with soap and water as soon as you can afterward, even if you wore gloves. This is not about being squeamish, it is standard practice for every trained responder, and it protects both you and the next person you help.

sections.heading: Good Samaritan Protection
body: In the United States, Good Samaritan laws in every state protect people who give reasonable, good-faith first aid from being sued if something goes wrong, as long as they are not reckless and do not go beyond their training. This means you are legally protected for stepping in to help.

The one firm rule: once you start care, do not leave the person until someone with equal or greater training takes over, or professional responders arrive. Stopping abruptly can be more harmful than not starting at all, except when the scene becomes unsafe.

keyTerms.def: Checking an area for hazards before entering it to help someone.
Treating all blood and body fluids as if they could carry infection, using gloves and barriers.
Legal protection for people who give reasonable emergency help in good faith.
Whether a person reacts to voice, touch, or pain; the first thing you check in an emergency.

practice.q: You find someone collapsed near a downed power line. What should you do first?
choices: Rush over and check their pulse
Stay back and call 911 without approaching the hazard
Move the power line out of the way
Shout for the person to move themselves
practice.explain: Scene safety comes before patient care. A live power line can injure or kill a rescuer, so you call for help and wait for trained responders to make the scene safe.

practice.q: Why do first responders put on gloves before treating a bleeding wound?
choices: Gloves make bleeding stop faster
Universal precautions protect against bloodborne infection
It is required by law in all situations
Gloves keep the wound sterile forever
practice.explain: Gloves and other barriers are part of universal precautions, which treat all blood and body fluids as potentially infectious to protect both the helper and the injured person.

practice.q: What do Good Samaritan laws generally protect?
choices: Anyone who touches an injured person
People who give reasonable, good-faith emergency help within their training
Only certified paramedics
People who film emergencies to share online
practice.explain: Good Samaritan laws protect bystanders who act reasonably and in good faith, not people who are reckless or who act far outside what they know how to do.

lessons.title: Primary Assessment and the Recovery Position
lessons.intro: Once a scene is safe, you need a fast, repeatable way to figure out how serious things are. Emergency responders call this the primary assessment, and you can learn the same core steps: check responsiveness, airway, and breathing, in that order, every time.

sections.heading: Responsiveness, Airway, Breathing
body: First, check responsiveness by tapping the shoulders and shouting. If there is no response, shout for someone to call 911 and bring an AED while you continue. Next, check the airway: if the person is on their back and unresponsive, gently tilt the head back and lift the chin to open the airway, which can be blocked by the tongue relaxing backward.

Then check breathing for no more than 10 seconds by looking at the chest and listening near the mouth. Normal breathing looks regular; occasional gasping, called agonal breathing, is not normal breathing and is a sign of cardiac arrest, not a reason to wait.

example.problem: You find an unresponsive adult lying on their back. You open the airway and watch the chest for 8 seconds. You see only one irregular gasp with a 6-second gap before it, and no other movement.
steps: Recognize that occasional gasping is agonal breathing, not normal breathing.
Treat agonal breathing the same as no breathing at all.
Conclude this person needs CPR, not the recovery position.
example.answer: This is cardiac arrest. Begin hands-only CPR immediately and make sure 911 has been called.

sections.heading: The Recovery Position
body: If a person is unresponsive but breathing normally, place them in the recovery position: roll them onto their side with the top leg bent forward for balance and the top hand supporting the head, tilting the chin slightly up to keep the airway open. This position lets fluids like vomit drain out of the mouth instead of down the airway.

Stay with the person, recheck their breathing every couple of minutes, and be ready to start CPR if breathing stops or becomes abnormal. Never leave an unresponsive but breathing person flat on their back and unattended.

keyTerms.def: The first fast check of responsiveness, airway, and breathing in an emergency.
Irregular, gasping breaths that are a sign of cardiac arrest, not real breathing.
A side-lying position that keeps the airway open and lets fluid drain from an unresponsive but breathing person.
A technique to open a blocked airway by tilting the head back and lifting the chin.

practice.q: An unresponsive person is breathing normally. What should you do?
choices: Start chest compressions immediately
Place them in the recovery position and monitor breathing
Give them water to drink
Leave them to call a family member
practice.explain: If someone is unresponsive but breathing normally, the recovery position protects their airway from fluids while you monitor them; CPR is only for someone not breathing normally.

practice.q: Why is agonal breathing treated as 'not breathing' in first aid?
choices: It sounds annoying
It is a sign of cardiac arrest, not effective breathing
It only happens in healthy people
It means the person is asleep
practice.explain: Agonal gasps are a reflex from a dying brainstem during cardiac arrest, not functional breathing, so they should trigger CPR rather than the recovery position.

practice.q: What is the correct order of the primary assessment?
choices: Breathing, airway, responsiveness
Airway, responsiveness, breathing
Responsiveness, airway, breathing
Call 911, breathing, responsiveness
practice.explain: You check responsiveness first, then open and check the airway, then check breathing, each step building on the last.

lessons.title: Calling 911 Effectively
lessons.intro: A phone call is one of the most powerful first aid tools you have, but only if you make it well. Dispatchers are trained to get critical information fast and can talk you through CPR or bleeding control step by step, so knowing how to work with them matters as much as knowing the skills yourself.

sections.heading: What to Say, in Order
body: Give the location first, including cross streets or a building name and floor, because if the call drops, that is the one detail dispatchers need most to send help. Then describe what happened: is the person breathing, conscious, bleeding heavily, or having chest pain? Answer the dispatcher's questions directly instead of repeating your own story.

Do not hang up until the dispatcher tells you to. Many dispatchers give real-time instructions, such as counting out loud for CPR compressions or explaining how to apply pressure to a wound, and hanging up early means losing that guidance exactly when you need it most.

sections.heading: When It Is Mental Health, Not Just Physical
body: Call 911 for immediate physical danger, such as someone who has overdosed, is unconscious, or is actively harming themselves. If instead someone is in emotional crisis, suicidal, or overwhelmed but not in immediate physical danger, the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline connects them with trained counselors by call or text, day or night.

You can also call 988 on someone else's behalf if you are worried about them, and the counselor can help you decide whether emergency services are needed. Knowing both numbers means you can match the response to the actual emergency.

keyTerms.def: The 911 call taker who gathers information and can give real-time first aid instructions.
The U.S. Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, reachable by call or text, for mental health emergencies.
The two intersecting streets nearest an emergency, useful for pinpointing location fast.

practice.q: What is the single most important detail to give a 911 dispatcher first?
choices: Your name
The location of the emergency
What insurance the person has
A full medical history
practice.explain: If the call is lost, dispatchers can still send help if they already have the location, so it is given first, before other details.

practice.q: When is 988 the better number to call instead of 911?
choices: When someone is in emotional crisis but not in immediate physical danger
When there is a house fire
When someone is unconscious
When someone is bleeding heavily
practice.explain: 988 connects callers to trained crisis counselors for suicidal thoughts or emotional crises; 911 is for immediate physical danger like fires, injuries, or unconsciousness.

practice.q: Why should you stay on the line with a 911 dispatcher instead of hanging up right away?
choices: It is required by law in every state
Dispatchers can give real-time instructions like CPR guidance
The call is free only if you stay on longer
Hanging up cancels the response
practice.explain: Dispatchers often coach callers through CPR, bleeding control, or choking response in real time, so staying on the line keeps that help available.

units.title: Life-Threatening Emergencies
units.summary: Cardiac arrest and choking can kill within minutes. This unit teaches the physical skills that keep a person alive until an AED or paramedics arrive: hands-only CPR, AED use, and clearing a blocked airway.

lessons.title: Hands-Only CPR for Adults
lessons.intro: When an adult's heart stops beating effectively, their brain starts losing oxygen within seconds and permanent damage can begin in as little as four to six minutes. Hands-only CPR keeps blood moving to the brain and heart until an AED or paramedics arrive, and you do not need to be certified to start it.

sections.heading: The Compressions Themselves
body: Kneel beside the person, place the heel of one hand on the center of the chest, over the lower half of the breastbone, and place your other hand on top with fingers interlaced. Keep your arms straight and your shoulders directly over your hands, and push using your body weight, not just your arms.

Push hard and fast: compress at least 2 inches (5 cm) deep for an adult, at a rate of 100 to 120 compressions per minute, which is close to the beat of the song "Stayin' Alive." Let the chest fully rise back up between compressions; this recoil lets the heart refill with blood before the next push.

example.problem: You are giving hands-only CPR and want to keep a steady, correct pace without a metronome.
steps: Recall the target rate: 100 to 120 compressions per minute.
Use a familiar song at that tempo, such as "Stayin' Alive" (about 103 beats per minute) or "Crazy in Love", as a mental beat.
Push to that beat, compressing at least 2 inches deep each time and letting the chest fully recoil.
example.answer: Matching compressions to a ~100-120 beat-per-minute song keeps you in the correct CPR rate without counting out loud the whole time.

sections.heading: Minimizing Interruptions
body: Every pause in compressions lets blood flow to the brain drop back toward zero, so keep interruptions under 10 seconds whenever possible, for example when switching rescuers or attaching an AED. If you get tired, ask a bystander to take over every two minutes, since compression quality drops with fatigue even if you do not feel tired yet.

Hands-only CPR (no rescue breaths) is recommended for untrained bystanders responding to an adult in cardiac arrest, because it is simpler to teach over the phone and studies show it works about as well as CPR with breaths for the first several minutes. Continue until an AED is ready to analyze, professional help takes over, or the person starts moving and breathing normally.

keyTerms.def: When the heart stops pumping blood effectively, distinct from a heart attack (a blockage in blood flow to the heart muscle).
Letting the chest fully rise back up between compressions so the heart can refill with blood.
Chest compressions only, without rescue breaths, recommended for untrained bystanders helping an adult.

practice.q: At what rate should you perform chest compressions on an adult?
choices: 40 to 60 per minute
100 to 120 per minute
150 to 180 per minute
As fast as physically possible
practice.explain: The target rate for adult chest compressions is 100 to 120 per minute, similar to the tempo of "Stayin' Alive."

practice.q: Why is full chest recoil important between compressions?
choices: It looks more professional
It lets the heart refill with blood before the next compression
It reduces the compression rate needed
It prevents the rescuer from getting tired
practice.explain: Full recoil allows the heart's chambers to refill between compressions, which is necessary for each compression to actually move blood.

practice.q: Why is hands-only CPR recommended for untrained bystanders?
choices: It requires no chest compressions at all
It is simpler, easier to guide by phone, and works about as well initially as CPR with breaths
It is only for children
It replaces the need to call 911
practice.explain: Hands-only CPR removes the rescue-breath step, making it easier for an untrained bystander to start immediately and to be coached through by a 911 dispatcher.

lessons.title: Using an AED
lessons.intro: An automated external defibrillator, or AED, can shock a heart out of a deadly rhythm and back into one that pumps blood. These devices are built for untrained bystanders: they talk you through every step and will not deliver a shock unless one is actually needed.

sections.heading: Turn It On and Follow the Voice Prompts
body: As soon as an AED arrives, turn it on before doing anything else; the voice prompts will guide the rest. Expose the person's bare chest, wipe away sweat or water if present, and attach the two pads exactly where the pictures on the pads show, usually upper right chest and lower left side.

The AED will then say "analyzing, do not touch the patient," and everyone must stop touching them so the machine can read the heart's rhythm accurately. If a shock is advised, the AED will tell everyone to stand clear and either deliver the shock automatically or ask you to press a button.

sections.heading: Resuming CPR After the Shock
body: Immediately after a shock (or if no shock is advised), resume chest compressions right away rather than checking for a pulse first; the heart usually needs continued CPR even after a successful shock to keep blood moving while it stabilizes. The AED will re-analyze the rhythm every two minutes and prompt you again.

Special cases: if the person has a hairy chest that prevents the pads from sticking, quickly shave the area with a razor if one is in the AED kit. If the person is lying in water, move them to a dry area first, since electricity and standing water do not mix safely for rescuers.

keyTerms.def: Automated External Defibrillator, a device that analyzes heart rhythm and can deliver a shock to restore a normal rhythm.
The phase where the AED reads the heart's electrical rhythm and no one should touch the patient.
Attaching AED pads to bare skin, typically upper right chest and lower left side, following the pictures on the pads.

practice.q: What should you do first when an AED arrives at the scene?
choices: Attach the pads before turning it on
Turn it on and follow its voice prompts
Check the person's pulse for 30 seconds
Wait for paramedics to operate it
practice.explain: AEDs are designed to be used immediately by bystanders; turning it on first lets the voice prompts guide every remaining step correctly.

practice.q: What should everyone do while the AED is analyzing the heart rhythm?
choices: Continue chest compressions
Stop touching the patient completely
Give rescue breaths
Remove the pads
practice.explain: Touching or moving the patient during analysis can produce a false reading, so the AED specifically instructs everyone to stop touching the patient while it analyzes.

practice.q: What should you do immediately after an AED delivers a shock?
choices: Check for a pulse for one full minute
Resume chest compressions right away
Turn the AED off
Wait five minutes before touching the person
practice.explain: Guidelines call for resuming CPR immediately after a shock (or a no-shock advice) rather than pausing to check a pulse, since the heart typically needs continued support.

lessons.title: Responding to Choking
lessons.intro: Choking can cut off a person's airway completely within seconds, and unlike cardiac arrest it often has a fast, physical fix a bystander can perform right away. Knowing the difference between a person who can still cough and one who cannot make a sound is the key decision point.

sections.heading: Recognizing Severe Choking
body: A person with a mild, partial airway blockage can still cough forcefully or speak; in this case, encourage them to keep coughing and do not intervene physically, since forceful coughing is the body's own most effective clearing mechanism. Severe choking looks different: the person cannot cough, speak, or breathe, may clutch their throat (the universal choking sign), and their lips or face may start to turn bluish.
Ask clearly, "Are you choking?" If they nod yes and cannot speak, treat it as severe choking and act immediately; do not wait to see if it resolves on its own.

sections.heading: Back Blows and Abdominal Thrusts
body: For a conscious adult with severe choking, stand slightly behind and to the side, support their chest with one hand, and give 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your other hand. If that does not clear the object, move to abdominal thrusts (the Heimlich maneuver): stand behind the person, wrap your arms around their waist, make a fist with one hand above the navel and well below the breastbone, grasp it with your other hand, and thrust inward and upward sharply.
Alternate 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts until the object is expelled, the person can breathe or cough forcefully again, or they become unresponsive.

example.problem: A person at a restaurant grabs their throat, cannot speak, and their face is turning blue. You confirm they are choking.
steps: Give 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades.
If the object is not cleared, give 5 abdominal thrusts above the navel.
Alternate sets of 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts until the airway clears or the person becomes unresponsive.
example.answer: Continue alternating back blows and abdominal thrusts in sets of 5 until the object comes out or the person stops responding, at which point you would begin CPR.

sections.heading: If the Person Becomes Unresponsive
body: If a choking person goes limp and unresponsive, carefully lower them to the ground and begin CPR, starting with chest compressions. Each time you open the airway to give a breath, look inside the mouth first; if you can see the object, remove it with your fingers, but never do a blind finger sweep when you cannot see anything.
Make sure 911 has been called as soon as severe choking is recognized, even if the object seems likely to clear quickly, because a person can go from choking to unresponsive within a minute or two.

keyTerms.def: Clutching the throat with one or both hands, the widely recognized signal for choking.
Also called the Heimlich maneuver; inward-and-upward thrusts above the navel to expel an airway obstruction.
Firm strikes between the shoulder blades used to dislodge a choking obstruction.

practice.q: A person is coughing forcefully and can still speak a few words. What should you do?
choices: Immediately give abdominal thrusts
Encourage them to keep coughing and do not intervene physically yet
Start CPR right away
Give back blows only
practice.explain: Forceful coughing means the airway is only partially blocked and the body's own cough reflex is the most effective way to clear it; physical intervention is for severe, complete blockage.

practice.q: What is the correct sequence for a conscious adult with severe choking?
choices: 10 abdominal thrusts only
Alternating 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts
Immediate CPR without checking responsiveness
A blind finger sweep of the mouth
practice.explain: The recommended technique alternates sets of 5 back blows with 5 abdominal thrusts until the obstruction clears or the person becomes unresponsive.

practice.q: Why should you never do a blind finger sweep in someone's mouth?
choices: It is against the law
You could push an unseen object further down the airway
It takes too much time
It is not part of any first aid guideline
practice.explain: Sweeping blindly can push an object deeper into the airway; you should only remove an object you can actually see.

units.title: Bleeding, Wounds, and Trauma
units.summary: Severe bleeding can be fatal in minutes, faster than most people expect. This unit covers stopping bleeding, dressing wounds, recognizing shock, and handling burns and broken bones.

lessons.title: Controlling Severe Bleeding
lessons.intro: An adult can lose a life-threatening amount of blood in just a few minutes from a severe wound, which is faster than most ambulances can arrive. The "Stop the Bleed" techniques taught to the public since 2015 - direct pressure, wound packing, and tourniquets - are simple enough for anyone to learn and can save a life before paramedics get there.

sections.heading: Direct Pressure First
body: For almost any bleeding wound, the first step is firm, direct pressure using a clean cloth, gauze, or even a shirt pressed straight down on the wound with both hands. Do not lift the cloth to check if bleeding has stopped; peeking disrupts any clot that is forming. If blood soaks through, add more material on top rather than removing the first layer.

Maintain steady pressure for at least 5 to 10 minutes without stopping, which feels like a long time but is often what it takes for a clot to hold. For a wound on an arm or leg, keeping the limb elevated above heart level can help reduce blood flow to the area while you maintain pressure.

sections.heading: Wound Packing for Deep Wounds
body: If a wound is too deep or wide for direct pressure alone to work, such as a deep gash where pressure on the surface does not reach the bleeding vessel, pack the wound: push gauze or clean cloth firmly down into the wound itself, filling the space, then apply direct pressure on top of the packed material.

This is uncomfortable for the injured person but is far less dangerous than continued severe blood loss. Keep packing and applying pressure continuously until help arrives; do not remove packing to check the wound.

sections.heading: When to Use a Tourniquet
body: If bleeding from an arm or leg is life-threatening and direct pressure and packing are not controlling it, apply a tourniquet 2 to 3 inches above the wound (never directly on a joint), tightening it until the bleeding stops, which will be quite tight and painful. Note the time you applied it, since responders need to know how long it has been on.

A tourniquet left on too long can damage the limb, but that risk is far smaller than the risk of bleeding to death, so once applied, only trained medical personnel should decide to loosen it. Commercial tourniquets work best; a wide, non-stretchy improvised band (like a folded bandana, never thin cord or wire) can work if nothing else is available.

example.problem: Someone has a deep laceration on the upper thigh that is spurting bright red blood. Direct pressure with a folded shirt for two minutes has not slowed the bleeding.
steps: Recognize this as life-threatening arterial bleeding that direct pressure alone is not controlling.
Apply a tourniquet 2 to 3 inches above the wound, not on the knee joint.
Tighten until bleeding stops completely, note the time applied, and call 911 immediately if not already done.
example.answer: Apply a tourniquet above the wound, tighten fully, record the time, and get the person to emergency care as fast as possible without loosening the tourniquet yourself.

keyTerms.def: Firm, steady force applied straight onto a wound to help blood clot and stop bleeding.
Pushing gauze or cloth into a deep wound to reach a bleeding vessel that surface pressure cannot control.
A tight band applied above a severely bleeding limb wound to cut off blood flow when other methods fail.
A national public campaign teaching bystanders direct pressure, wound packing, and tourniquet use.

practice.q: Why should you avoid lifting a dressing to check if bleeding has stopped?
choices: It wastes gauze
It can disrupt a forming clot
It is against Stop the Bleed guidelines for legal reasons
It makes the wound look worse
practice.explain: Peeking under a dressing can pull apart a blood clot that is just beginning to form, restarting the bleeding you were trying to stop.

practice.q: Where should a tourniquet be placed relative to a bleeding wound on a leg?
choices: Directly on the wound
2 to 3 inches above the wound, not on a joint
Below the wound, toward the foot
Anywhere on the same limb
practice.explain: A tourniquet is placed a few inches above the wound, avoiding joints, so it can fully compress the blood vessels feeding the injury.

practice.q: Once a tourniquet has been applied and tightened, who should loosen it?
choices: The rescuer, after 10 minutes
Only trained medical personnel
The injured person, if they feel numbness
It should be loosened every 5 minutes to restore circulation
practice.explain: A properly applied tourniquet should stay in place until trained medical personnel evaluate the injury; loosening it too early can restart life-threatening bleeding.

lessons.title: Wound Care and Recognizing Shock
lessons.intro: Most wounds you will see day to day are not life-threatening, but they still need to be cleaned and dressed correctly to avoid infection, and every rescuer should be able to spot the early warning signs of shock, a dangerous drop in blood flow to the body's organs.

sections.heading: Cleaning and Dressing Minor Wounds
body: For a minor cut or scrape once bleeding has stopped, rinse the wound gently with clean running water to remove dirt and debris, then pat dry with a clean cloth. Apply a thin layer of antibiotic ointment if available, and cover with a sterile adhesive bandage or gauze secured with tape, sized to fully cover the wound.

Change the dressing daily or whenever it gets wet or dirty, and watch for signs of infection over the following days: increasing redness spreading outward, warmth, swelling, pus, red streaking, or fever. Any of these signs means the person should see a medical provider.

sections.heading: Recognizing Shock
body: Shock happens when the body's organs are not getting enough blood flow, often from severe bleeding, a bad allergic reaction, or serious infection. Watch for pale, cool, clammy skin, a rapid weak pulse, fast shallow breathing, confusion or anxiety, and complaints of thirst or nausea. Shock can develop even before blood pressure visibly drops, so do not wait for someone to look obviously unwell.

To manage shock while waiting for help: have the person lie down, keep them warm with a blanket, and if there is no suspected head, neck, back, or leg injury, raise their legs about 12 inches to help blood return toward the vital organs. Do not give them food or water, since they may need surgery and an empty stomach matters for anesthesia.

example.problem: A person injured in a fall is pale, sweating, breathing quickly, and says they feel dizzy and thirsty, though the visible wound looks minor.
steps: Recognize pale, clammy skin, rapid breathing, and thirst as signs of shock, not just a minor injury.
Call 911 if not already done, since shock is a medical emergency regardless of how the wound looks.
Lay the person down, keep them warm, and raise their legs about 12 inches if there is no suspected spine or leg injury.
example.answer: Treat this as shock: call for help, keep the person lying down and warm, elevate the legs if safe to do so, and do not give food or water.

keyTerms.def: A dangerous drop in blood flow to the body's organs, which can occur from severe bleeding, allergic reaction, or infection.
Spreading redness, warmth, swelling, pus, red streaking, or fever appearing after a wound.
Cool, pale, and sweaty skin, a common early sign of shock.

practice.q: Which of these is a warning sign of shock?
choices: Warm, dry, flushed skin and a slow pulse
Pale, cool, clammy skin with a rapid weak pulse
Normal breathing and calm mood
Increased appetite and thirst satisfied easily
practice.explain: Shock typically presents with pale, cool, clammy skin, a fast weak pulse, and rapid breathing, as the body redirects blood flow away from the skin and toward vital organs.

practice.q: Why should you not give food or water to someone showing signs of shock?
choices: It has no real medical reason, it is just a myth
They may need surgery, and an empty stomach matters for anesthesia
Food and water make bleeding worse directly
It is only a concern for children
practice.explain: If the person needs emergency surgery, having food or liquid in the stomach increases risks during anesthesia, so rescuers withhold food and water from someone in shock.

practice.q: Which of these is a sign that a wound has become infected?
choices: The scab has fully formed
Spreading redness, warmth, and pus around the wound
The wound itches slightly while healing
The bandage needed to be changed once
practice.explain: Increasing redness that spreads outward, warmth, swelling, and pus are classic signs of infection and mean the person should seek medical care.

lessons.title: Burns, Sprains, and Fractures
lessons.intro: Burns and broken bones look dramatic, but the first aid response for both comes down to a few clear rules: cool a burn quickly, protect a break without trying to fix it, and know which injuries need an ambulance instead of a bag of ice.

sections.heading: Classifying and Treating Burns
body: A first-degree burn, like most sunburns, is red and painful with no blisters, and affects only the outer layer of skin. A second-degree burn goes deeper, causing blisters and intense pain. A third-degree burn destroys all layers of skin, can look white, charred, or leathery, and may feel numb because nerve endings have been destroyed.

For first- and second-degree burns, cool the area under cool (not ice-cold) running water for 10 to 20 minutes, remove jewelry or tight clothing near the area before swelling starts, and cover loosely with a clean, dry, non-stick dressing. Never pop blisters, and never apply butter, oil, or ice directly to a burn, which can trap heat or damage tissue further.

Any third-degree burn, a burn covering a large area, or a burn to the face, hands, feet, groin, or a major joint needs emergency care. Call 911, cover the area loosely with a clean dry cloth, and do not remove clothing that is stuck to the burn.

sections.heading: Sprains and Strains: RICE
body: A sprain is a stretched or torn ligament (connecting bone to bone), often at an ankle or wrist; a strain involves a muscle or tendon. Both typically cause pain, swelling, and bruising without an obvious deformity. The classic first aid response is RICE: Rest the area, Ice it for 15-20 minutes at a time with a cloth between ice and skin, Compress with an elastic bandage snug but not numbing, and Elevate the limb above heart level when possible.
See a medical provider if the person cannot bear any weight on the injury, if there is significant deformity, or if numbness or a cold, pale foot or hand suggests reduced blood flow.

sections.heading: Splinting a Suspected Fracture
body: If you suspect a broken bone, the core rule is: splint it in the position you found it, do not try to straighten or realign the limb. Immobilize the joint above and below the injury using a rigid object (a rolled magazine, a board, even a sturdy stick) padded and secured with cloth strips or tape, snug enough to prevent movement but not so tight it cuts off circulation.

Check fingers or toes beyond the splint periodically for color, warmth, and feeling; if they turn pale, cold, or numb, the splint is too tight and needs to be loosened. Call 911 for any suspected fracture of the skull, spine, ribs, hip, or thigh, or for any open fracture where bone has broken through skin.

example.problem: A hiker falls and their lower leg is now bent at an unnatural angle below the knee, with visible swelling, but the skin is not broken.
steps: Do not attempt to straighten or realign the leg.
Splint the leg in the position found, immobilizing the joints above (knee) and below (ankle) using padded rigid supports.
Check toes for color, warmth, and sensation after splinting, and call 911 for transport.
example.answer: Splint the leg exactly as found, immobilize above and below the injury, monitor circulation in the toes, and get emergency transport since this is a suspected long-bone fracture.

keyTerms.def: A burn affecting only the outer skin layer, red and painful with no blisters.
A burn destroying all skin layers, which can appear white, charred, or leathery and may be numb.
Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation - the standard first aid approach to sprains and strains.
A rigid support used to immobilize a suspected fracture in the position it was found.

practice.q: How should you cool a first- or second-degree burn?
choices: Apply ice directly to the burn
Run cool (not ice-cold) water over it for 10 to 20 minutes
Cover it in butter or oil
Pop any blisters first
practice.explain: Cool running water for 10 to 20 minutes reduces heat in the tissue safely; ice can damage tissue further and butter or oil can trap heat and increase infection risk.

practice.q: What is the core rule when splinting a suspected fracture?
choices: Straighten the limb before splinting
Splint it in the position it was found
Only immobilize the joint closest to the body
Wait until swelling goes down before splinting
practice.explain: Rescuers should splint a suspected fracture in the position found, immobilizing the joints above and below, rather than attempting to realign the bone themselves.

practice.q: Which burn requires calling 911 immediately?
choices: A small first-degree sunburn on the shoulder
A third-degree burn or one affecting the face, hands, or groin
Mild redness after touching a warm plate
A blister-free burn the size of a coin
practice.explain: Third-degree burns and burns to sensitive or high-risk areas like the face, hands, feet, groin, or major joints need emergency medical care.

units.title: Environmental and Medical Emergencies
units.summary: Heat, cold, allergies, seizures, strokes, and overdoses all have distinct warning signs and distinct first responses. This unit ties the course together with the emergencies you are most likely to encounter outside of trauma.

lessons.title: Heat and Cold Emergencies
lessons.intro: The body works hard to keep its core temperature near 98.6°F (37°C), and when heat or cold overwhelms that system, the results range from uncomfortable to life-threatening within a fairly short window. Telling the milder stage from the dangerous stage is the key skill in this lesson.

sections.heading: Heat Exhaustion vs. Heat Stroke
body: Heat exhaustion shows up as heavy sweating, weakness, cool and clammy skin, a fast weak pulse, nausea, and headache. Move the person to a cooler place, loosen clothing, apply cool wet cloths, and have them sip water if fully alert. They should improve within about 30 minutes; if not, or if symptoms worsen, seek medical care.

Heat stroke is a medical emergency: body temperature above 103°F (39.4°C), hot skin that may be red and dry or damp, a fast strong pulse, confusion, and possible loss of consciousness. Call 911 immediately, move the person to shade or air conditioning, and cool them as fast as possible with cold water immersion or ice packs to the neck, armpits, and groin. Do not give fluids if they are confused or unconscious, due to choking risk.

sections.heading: Hypothermia and Frostbite
body: Hypothermia begins with shivering, but as core temperature keeps dropping, shivering can actually stop, along with confusion, slurred speech, drowsiness, and slow breathing, which is a dangerous sign, not a good one. Move the person to warmth, remove wet clothing, wrap them in dry blankets, and if they are fully alert, offer warm sweet drinks (never alcohol). Handle them gently, since a very cold heart can be sensitive to rough movement.

Frostbite affects skin and tissue directly, showing numbness and skin that turns pale, waxy, or grayish and feels hard or firm. Move to warmth, remove wet or tight clothing and jewelry, and rewarm gently in warm (not hot) water around 99-102°F (37-39°C); never rub the area, which can damage frozen tissue further, and never rewarm if there is a chance of refreezing, which causes worse damage than staying frozen a bit longer.

example.problem: A hiker's fingers are numb, look grayish-white, and feel hard, but there is a risk of temperatures dropping again before reaching shelter.
steps: Recognize signs of frostbite: numbness, pale/gray waxy skin, firmness.
Decide whether rewarming now risks refreezing before reaching a stable warm environment.
If refreezing is likely, protect the area and keep it as warm as possible without full rewarming until true shelter is reached; if shelter is secure, rewarm gently in warm (not hot) water.
example.answer: Avoid rewarming until you can guarantee no refreezing, since refreezing thawed tissue causes more damage than delaying rewarming until reaching stable shelter.

keyTerms.def: A heat-related illness with heavy sweating, weakness, and clammy skin, treatable by cooling and rest.
A life-threatening emergency with body temperature above 103°F, hot skin, and confusion, requiring 911 and rapid cooling.
Dangerously low core body temperature; late signs include shivering stopping, confusion, and drowsiness.
Freezing injury to skin and tissue, showing numbness and pale, waxy, hard skin.

practice.q: Which symptom set signals heat stroke rather than heat exhaustion?
choices: Heavy sweating and mild nausea
Body temperature over 103°F, hot skin, and confusion
Slight headache and thirst
Cool clammy skin with a fast weak pulse
practice.explain: Heat stroke involves a very high core temperature, hot skin, and altered mental status like confusion, and is a 911 emergency, unlike the milder presentation of heat exhaustion.

practice.q: What is a dangerous, easy-to-misread sign of worsening hypothermia?
choices: Increased shivering
Shivering stopping while confusion sets in
Sweating heavily
Rapid, strong pulse
practice.explain: As hypothermia worsens, the body may stop shivering, which can be mistaken for improvement but actually signals the condition is getting more severe.

practice.q: Why should you never rub frostbitten skin?
choices: It has no effect either way
Rubbing can cause further damage to frozen tissue
It warms the skin too quickly
It is only a concern for burns, not frostbite
practice.explain: Ice crystals in frozen tissue can cause additional damage if the area is rubbed, so gentle warming in warm water is preferred over friction.

lessons.title: Allergic Reactions, Seizures, and Stroke
lessons.intro: Anaphylaxis, seizures, and stroke can each turn dangerous within minutes, and each has its own unmistakable pattern once you know what to look for. This lesson gives you the recognition cues and the specific first response for all three.

sections.heading: Anaphylaxis
body: Anaphylaxis is a severe, whole-body allergic reaction, often to foods, insect stings, or medications, that can include hives, swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat, difficulty breathing, a drop in blood pressure, and a rapid weak pulse. It can become fatal within minutes if the airway swells shut.

If the person has an epinephrine auto-injector (such as an EpiPen), help them use it right away: remove the safety cap, press firmly against the outer thigh (through clothing is fine) until it clicks, and hold for about 3 seconds. Call 911 immediately even if symptoms improve, because a second wave of symptoms can occur, and a second dose may be needed after 5 to 15 minutes if there is no improvement and another injector is available.

sections.heading: Seizures
body: During a seizure, protect the person from injury by clearing hard or sharp objects away and cushioning their head, but do not restrain their movements and never put anything in their mouth. Time the seizure from when it starts.

Call 911 if the seizure lasts longer than 5 minutes, if another seizure starts right after the first, if the person is injured, pregnant, or has diabetes, if it happens in water, or if they do not regain consciousness afterward. Once convulsions stop, roll the person into the recovery position and stay with them until they are fully alert, since confusion afterward is normal and can last several minutes.

sections.heading: Stroke: the FAST Test
body: A stroke happens when blood flow to part of the brain is blocked or a blood vessel bleeds, and brain cells begin dying within minutes, so speed matters enormously. Use the FAST test: Face - ask them to smile and look for one side drooping; Arm - ask them to raise both arms and look for one drifting downward; Speech - ask them to repeat a simple sentence and listen for slurring or wrong words; Time - if any of these are abnormal, call 911 immediately and note the time symptoms started.

The time symptoms began matters medically, because clot-dissolving treatment is generally only effective within the first few hours, so telling paramedics the exact time can directly affect what treatment options are available.

example.problem: A coworker suddenly cannot lift their right arm as high as their left, and their speech sounds slightly slurred when they answer a question, though they insist they are fine.
steps: Apply the FAST test: Face (check for drooping), Arm (uneven raising, confirmed), Speech (slurred, confirmed).
Recognize two abnormal FAST findings as enough to act, regardless of the person's own assessment.
Call 911 immediately and note the exact time the symptoms were first noticed.
example.answer: This is a likely stroke. Call 911 right away, note the time symptoms started, and do not wait to see if it passes, since treatment windows are time-limited.

keyTerms.def: A severe, potentially fatal whole-body allergic reaction that can cause airway swelling and low blood pressure.
A spring-loaded device that delivers a dose of epinephrine into the outer thigh to treat anaphylaxis.
Face, Arm, Speech, Time - a quick check used to recognize a possible stroke.
A side-lying position used after a seizure ends to keep the airway clear while consciousness returns.

practice.q: Where should an epinephrine auto-injector be administered?
choices: Into a vein in the arm
Firmly against the outer thigh
Under the tongue
Into the abdomen only
practice.explain: Epinephrine auto-injectors are designed to be pressed firmly against the outer thigh, and they work through clothing if necessary.

practice.q: What should you do while someone is actively convulsing during a seizure?
choices: Hold their arms and legs still
Put a spoon or cloth in their mouth
Clear hazards away, cushion their head, and do not restrain them
Give them water to drink
practice.explain: You should protect a seizing person from injury by clearing the area and cushioning the head, without restraining movement or putting anything in the mouth, both of which can cause harm.

practice.q: In the FAST stroke test, what does the 'T' remind you to do?
choices: Take their temperature
Note the time symptoms started and call 911 immediately
Time how long they can hold their arms up
Wait ten minutes to confirm symptoms are real
practice.explain: The T in FAST stands for Time: noting when symptoms began and calling 911 right away, since stroke treatment is time-sensitive.

lessons.title: Poisoning, Overdose, and Your First Aid Kit
lessons.intro: This closing lesson covers two emergencies where the right first response can be the difference between life and death - poisoning and opioid overdose - and ends with the practical step of building a kit so you are actually ready to use everything you have learned.

sections.heading: Poisoning
body: If someone has swallowed, inhaled, or been exposed to a poison and is conscious and alert, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 in the United States for free, expert, 24/7 guidance specific to the substance involved; they will tell you whether home care, a specific antidote, or an emergency room visit is needed. Do not induce vomiting unless a poison control specialist or 911 dispatcher specifically tells you to.

Call 911 immediately instead of Poison Control if the person is unconscious, having trouble breathing, having a seizure, or cannot be woken. If safe to do so, keep the container or packaging of whatever was ingested, since it helps responders identify the substance and dose quickly.

sections.heading: Recognizing and Responding to Opioid Overdose
body: Signs of an opioid overdose include pinpoint (very small) pupils, slow or stopped breathing, blue or gray lips and fingertips, limpness, and unresponsiveness to voice or a firm sternal rub. Call 911 immediately, since this is a life-threatening emergency.

If naloxone (commonly known by the brand Narcan) is available, give it as a nasal spray by inserting the tip into one nostril and pressing the plunger; it works within minutes to temporarily reverse opioid effects on breathing. Begin rescue breathing or CPR if the person is not breathing, and stay with them, since naloxone can wear off before the opioid does, meaning breathing can slow again and a second dose (after 2-3 minutes) or more CPR may be needed.

example.problem: You find someone unresponsive with very small pupils and slow, shallow breathing. A naloxone nasal spray is available nearby.
steps: Call 911 immediately - this is a life-threatening emergency.
Administer the naloxone nasal spray into one nostril per its instructions.
Begin rescue breathing or CPR if breathing is inadequate, and be ready to give a second dose after 2-3 minutes if there is no improvement.
example.answer: Call 911, give naloxone right away, support breathing with rescue breaths or CPR as needed, and stay until paramedics arrive since a second dose may be necessary.

sections.heading: Building a First Aid Kit
body: A useful kit includes adhesive bandages in several sizes, sterile gauze pads and a roll of gauze, medical tape, antiseptic wipes, antibiotic ointment, tweezers (for splinters and stingers), trauma shears, disposable gloves, a CPR face shield, an elastic bandage for sprains, an instant cold pack, and a space blanket. Add any personal medications, like an epinephrine auto-injector or naloxone if relevant to your household, plus a card with emergency contacts.

Check your kit every six months: replace expired medications and ointments, restock anything used, and make sure gloves have not degraded. A kit that has never been checked is often missing exactly what you need when an emergency actually happens.

keyTerms.def: A free 24/7 U.S. hotline (1-800-222-1222) providing expert guidance for poisoning exposures.
A medication (brand name Narcan) that can temporarily reverse the effects of an opioid overdose.
Firmly rubbing the knuckles on the breastbone to check for responsiveness in someone who is not reacting to voice.

practice.q: When should you call Poison Control instead of 911 for a poisoning exposure?
choices: When the person is unconscious
When the person is conscious, alert, and not having breathing trouble
Never - always call 911 for any poisoning
Only for poisonings involving children
practice.explain: Poison Control (1-800-222-1222) is for conscious, stable patients needing guidance on a specific exposure; 911 is for unconscious, non-breathing, or seizing patients.

practice.q: What are classic signs of an opioid overdose?
choices: Wide, dilated pupils and fast breathing
Pinpoint pupils, slow or stopped breathing, and blue lips
High fever and rapid heart rate
Excessive thirst and confusion
practice.explain: Opioid overdose typically causes pinpoint pupils, slowed or stopped breathing, and bluish lips or fingertips from lack of oxygen.

practice.q: Why might a second dose of naloxone be needed after the first?
choices: Naloxone is never effective the first time
Naloxone's effects can wear off before the opioid's effects do
The first dose only treats pain, not breathing
It is required by law to give two doses
practice.explain: Naloxone works for a limited time and can wear off while the opioid is still active, so breathing can slow again, requiring another dose or continued rescue breathing.
